label: Preparation for the Local Theory
notes: This lecture spans printed pages 33 through 39 and gathers the non-symplectic machinery that later normal-form theorems consume. Frame the hour as a pipeline: a moving family of maps yields a vector field, the field differentiates pullbacks, a tubular neighborhood localizes, and a homotopy operator delivers exact primitives for Moser.

label: Isotopies
notes: Define an isotopy as a smooth one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms starting at the identity. Stress that we never freeze a single map; we track the whole path. The derivative of this path at each instant is the data we actually compute with, so the path is the object, not any one frame.

label: Time-Dependent Vector Fields
notes: Differentiating the isotopy in time produces a time-dependent vector field read at the moved point. Emphasize the composition order in the flow equation: the field is evaluated where the point has already gone. Conversely, integrating a complete time-dependent field recovers the isotopy, so the two encodings are equivalent.

label: The Lie Derivative
notes: Introduce the Lie derivative as the infinitesimal rate of change of a form dragged along a flow. Give the limit definition through the pullback, then note it measures how a tensor fails to be invariant under the flow. This is the bridge between the geometry of motion and the algebra of differential forms.

label: Cartan's Magic Formula
notes: Present Cartan's formula as the engine of the whole lecture: the Lie derivative splits into an exact piece and a contraction of the exterior derivative. Walk through why each term appears and stress that it lets us trade a flow derivative for purely algebraic operations on forms.

label: Differentiating Pullbacks
notes: For a time-dependent form pulled back along an isotopy, the time derivative carries two terms: the Lie derivative of the spatial part plus the explicit time derivative of the form. Warn students that forgetting the explicit term is the most common error and is exactly what the Moser equation balances.

label: The Homotopy Formula
notes: State the chain-homotopy formula relating the pullbacks at the two endpoints through an operator built by integrating the contraction along the flow. Show that the operator Q satisfies the identity minus pullback equals dQ plus Qd, the algebraic shadow of the geometric homotopy.

label: The Poincare Lemma
notes: Apply the homotopy formula on a contractible set: contracting to a point makes one endpoint pullback vanish on positive-degree forms, so every closed form becomes exact. Stress that this is local exactness, the precise tool that produces primitives for nearby forms in the Moser argument.

label: Tubular Neighborhoods
notes: Introduce the tubular neighborhood theorem: a neighborhood of a submanifold is diffeomorphic to a neighborhood of the zero section of its normal bundle. The radial contraction of fibers then makes the submanifold a deformation retract, supplying the homotopy the Poincare argument needs near a submanifold.

label: Projection Failure Mode
notes: Use the circle picture to show the hypothesis bites: the center is equidistant from every boundary point, so nearest-point projection is not unique once the radius is too large. This is why the theorem demands a sufficiently small, or shrinking, normal neighborhood in the noncompact case.

label: Assembling the Moser Trick
notes: Close by chaining the pieces: isotopy gives a field, Cartan differentiates the pullback, the tubular retract supplies a homotopy, and the homotopy formula yields an exact primitive. That primitive is precisely the input the next lecture feeds into the Moser equation to compare nearby forms.
